title: Fallback escape hatches and scaleback playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a compact, pragmatic playbook for dealing with inference-level overload and partial degradation across regions and capacity tiers. The idea is to provide a set of escape hatches and an ordered scaleback runway so apps stay alive and SLOs degrade predictably instead of falling off a cliff.

Intended audience: platform engineers, oncall SREs, and solutions engineers who configure customer routing policies.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Keep tail-latency and error-rate within acceptable bounds for core routes.
- Expose predictable, measurable degradation steps (so customers can set expectations).
- Minimize silent quality regressions by making every downgrade explicit and reversible.
- Allow fast manual intervention plus automated, conservative escalation when safe.

Key concepts (terminology):
- Escape hatch: a small, well-tested intervention that can be applied quickly to reduce load or cost while preserving core value. Examples: drop non-essential features, shorten context, route to cached/summary responses.
- Scaleback runway: an ordered sequence of degradation steps we apply when capacity pressure persists. Steps are monotonic in cost/latency reduction and ideally minimally invasive to UX.
- Soft-drop vs hard-drop: soft-drop preserves partial response (e.g., shorter generation); hard-drop returns a stub or redirects to a safe fallback. Prefer soft-drop when possible.

Scaleback levels (recommended canonical set):
- Level 0 (nominal): normal routing, full model family, caching enabled.
- Level 1 (mild pressure): aggressive batching and prefix caching, smaller KV cache TTL, enable partial-response hinting (client-side UI to stream skeleton then full text).
- Level 2 (moderate): automatic model variant swap to lower-cost quantized variant (same family if quality acceptable), context window trim heuristics, token-budget enforcement (per-request).
- Level 3 (severe): region spillover invoked (route to sibling region or dedicated fallback cluster), reduce max_tokens, prefer STATIC summaries/canned responses for low-importance prompts.
- Level 4 (emergency): circuit-break on non-critical routes (HTTP 503 with Retry-After), force degraded mode for all best-effort endpoints, enable manual operator overrides.

Escape hatches (catalog and guidance):
1) Token budget enforcement (fast, low-risk)
   - Enforce max_tokens on incoming requests by policy tier.
   - Use application hints to downgrade completion mode to terse.
   - Good for bursty traffic where each request is large.
2) Context trimming heuristics
   - Drop oldest messages or low-signal segments from history based on score.
   - Apply lightweight summarization on long contexts (cache summary) before forwarding.
3) Model variant downgrade
   - Swap to a quantized or distilled variant kept warmed for fast switch.
   - Only allowed when validation checks (quality gate) pass on a recent sample set.
4) Partial-render (soft-drop)
   - Return a shorter top-K tokens and schedule async enrich if needed.
   - Client can request full render later; useful for UI-first experiences.
5) Cached fallback responses
   - Static answers for high-frequency queries; must be versioned and audited.
6) Priority lanes and circuit-breakers
   - High-priority tokens (auth/system) bypass scaleback.
   - Lower-priority lanes get progressively stricter limits and eventually 503s.
7) Regional spillover with capacity scoring
   - Forward overflow to nearby regions with spare capacity; each region advertises a capacity score.

Control plane signals and policy wiring (what to monitor):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 across route/model; absolute values and delta-1m vs baseline
- Queue depth: request queue length per model instance and per-region
- GPU utilization and GPU wait (memory pressure, OOMs)
- Token throughput and token failure rate (e.g., partially generated responses)
- Error types: timeouts, OOM, preemption, internal 5xx
- Cost signal: current spend rate vs budget window for dedicated tenants
- Quality signal: automated regressions from eval prompts (sampled)

Recommended policy wiring:
- Alert A (yellow): p95 > threshold for 3 consecutive 1m windows -> move to Level 1
- Alert B (amber): queue depth > threshold OR GPU util > 85% for 2m -> move to Level 2
- Alert C (red): sustained error-rate > 1% or any OOM -> move to Level 3 and run regional spillover
- Manual trigger: oncall may escalate any route to Level 4 at their discretion

Routing policies and model variant selection (practical knobs):
- Token-aware routing: compute effective cost estimate = expected_tokens * cost_per_token(model). Prefer model variants with lower cost_per_token when under pressure.
- Priority routing map: bind customer routes to priority classes (system, premium, normal, best-effort). Each class has independent scaleback runway and SLA tail.
- Model-family affinity: prefer same-family downgrades (GPT-like -> quantized GPT-like) to reduce semantic regressions.
- Staggered spillover: avoid blasting single secondary region. Do progressive fan-out: 10% -> 30% -> 100% based on capacity score.

Multi-region spillover policy (operator-friendly recipe):
1) Evaluate regional capacity score: (available_gpus_weighted + spare_qps) / expected_load.
2) If primary < 0.6 and sibling > 1.2 => shift N% of traffic where N increases along scaleback runway.
3) Maintain sticky sessions for conversational contexts: use affinity window; when a session is moved, persist KV cache pointer to the target region.
4) If multiple regions under pressure, fall back to dedicated fallback clusters (warm, cheaper models).
5) Apply cross-region throttles to protect egress / network e2e latency budgets.

Control plane implementation notes (minimal, pragmatic):
- Represent policy as a small state machine per route: {level:int, last_transition_iso_ts:string, reason:string}. Keep this in a control plane store (Redis or small metadata DB).
- Use optimistic automation: automated transitions only happen if the metric condition persists for 2 sequential evaluation ticks (configurable).
- All automated transitions write an audit event with before/after and source metric snapshot.
- Expose an HTTP API for manual overrides plus a CLI for oncall.

Operational playbook (oncall steps):
1) Detection: review dashboard and alerts; capture last 10 error traces and recent model switches.
2) Verify scope: identify affected routes, tenant(s), and regions.
3) Apply first-line escapes: enable token caps and Level 1 batching tweaks.
4) If steady-state does not improve in 3m, escalate to Level 2 and enable model variant downgrade for non-SLA routes.
5) If regional pressure detected, open regional-spill ticket and progressively shift traffic (10/30/100).
6) Communicate: post an incident stub to #prod-incidents with status, scope, mitigation, and ETA.
7) Post-incident: run a quick regression eval on a small prompt corpus and capture quality deltas caused by model downgrades.

Quick checklist for runbook entries (copyable):
- [ ] snapshot dashboards (latency, queue depth, GPU util)
- [ ] list of affected routes and customer tiers
- [ ] which model variants are currently active (ids)
- [ ] last config changes and rollouts (link PR)
- [ ] apply Level X escape and timestamp it
- [ ] if spillover used, note target region and percent
- [ ] record manual overrides and reason
- [ ] open post-incident ticket for follow-up work

Example policy snippet (pseudo-yaml for CI checks / operator reference):
policy: "scaleback-runway-v1"
routes: [customer-chat, sys-annotate]
priority_classes:
  premium: {levels: [0,1,2], spillover: false}
  normal: {levels: [0,1,2,3], spillover: true}
  best-effort: {levels: [0,1,2,3,4], spillover: true}
triggers:
  p95_latency: {level1: 800ms, level2: 1200ms, level3: 2000ms}
  queue_depth: {level2: 60, level3: 120}
actions:
  level1: [enable_aggressive_batching, tighten_cache_ttl]
  level2: [switch_variant: "gptx-lite-q4", enable_token_cap]
  level3: [spillover: true, reduce_max_tokens]
  level4: [circuit_break_low_priority]

Caveats and risk notes:
- Downgrading models can introduce silent quality regressions. Always gate automated model swaps behind a small sample check or a conservative fallback that can be reversed quickly.
- Sticky conversational state across regions increases complexity (KV pointers, latency). Prefer best-effort continuity with clear client-side signals when moving sessions.
- Egress costs: multi-region spillover increases egress and cross-region storage pressure; account for cost in the decision function.

Open questions / backlog items:
- Should we maintain a small pool of warmed quantized variants per popular model family or spin them up on demand? (tradeoff: cost vs switch-time)
- Do we want per-tenant custom scaleback runways (some enterprise customers may accept deeper degradation)?
- How do we best capture customer-perceived quality regressions automatically (client-side metrics + synthetic probes)?
- Can we provide a developer-visible contract for "degradation semantics" so clients can gracefully adapt?

Next steps (short term):
- Prototype state-machine in runtime control plane (RD-2410) and add audit events (owner: Tomás)
- Add quick UI toggles in Console for Level 1/2 transitions (owner: Maya)
- Create a small benchmark harness to measure quality delta for the top 50 customer prompts when switching to quantized variants (owner: Elliot)

References and helpful links:
- internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/412
- confluence:Fallback_Control_Plane_v2 (design doc)
- JIRA: JIRA-RD-2410 (control-plane scaleback prototype)

Notes to self / friction points observed in experiments:
- Warm-up time for q4 variants varied wildly by model size; pre-warm policy needs smarter predictions (not just simple LRU).
- Some customers expect exact-turn continuity; need mapping in client SDK to indicate degraded mode.

If you are oncall: follow the checklist and ping me (Aisha) in #platform-ops if you need a manual override.

End of doc.
